balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

nim.title: Net interest margin
nim.content:
NIM is net interest income as a percentage of interest-earning assets.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the core profitability metric of a lender; a few basis points move earnings materially.

What to watch:

  • NIM trend with the rate cycle
  • Funding cost versus lending yield

loansDeposits.title: Gross loans and total deposits
loansDeposits.content:
Gross loans & advances is the total lending book before provisions; total deposits is customer and wholesale funding raised to fund it. The ratio of the two is the loan-to-deposit ratio, a core funding-mix gauge for a bank.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the retail mortgage book has been deliberately shrinking (system-wide BOQ+ME home lending down roughly 7.6% YTD to Feb-2026, and as much as ~22.7% in the legacy/broker book) as management runs off lower-returning loans, while Business Bank lending grows above system (~7-9%) in healthcare, agribusiness and secured commercial property. The blended gross loan book shown here nets those two moves against each other.

What to watch:

  • Whether Business Bank growth is large enough yet to offset the mortgage run-off and turn the total loan book back to growth (management guides to FY27)
  • Deposits funding loans 1:1 or better -- a loan-to-deposit ratio drifting above 100% signals rising reliance on wholesale funding
  • Deposit competition from the Big Four (now including ANZ-Suncorp) and digital-native challengers compressing the funding side

cashVsStatutory.title: Cash earnings vs statutory net income
cashVsStatutory.content:
Cash earnings is management's preferred profit measure, adjusting statutory NPAT for items like hedging volatility, amortisation of acquired intangibles and one-off gains/losses (e.g. goodwill impairments). Statutory net income is the audited bottom line.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: FY2025 statutory NPAT was $133m against cash earnings of $383m -- the gap driven mainly by a goodwill impairment, not a change in underlying trading. The DCF's owner-FCF base is built from cash earnings, since the statutory line in an impairment year would understate what the bank can sustainably distribute.

What to watch:

  • Whether the cash/statutory gap is a recurring feature (a red flag) or a one-off (as in FY2025)
  • Cash earnings growth versus the cost-to-income ratio and impairment expense trend

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Bank of Queensland Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
